name: Moundang (Kaélé)
overview: In the majority around Kaélé (“near the water”), the Moundang live alongside the Guiziga, Fulani and Toupouri. Coming from Sudan via Léré, in Chad, with which they share festivals, initiation and kingship, they obey a sovereign, the gon, surrounded by eleven notables. The guinarou, a great male initiation, and the biennial Gbeza festival punctuate their lives.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, neighbouring the Guiziga, the Fulani and the Toupouri, many of whom also speak Toupouri, Fulfulde and Guiziga.
Moundang is also spoken in Chad.
Long endogamous (exogamy was refused until around 1950), the group opened up after independence with the mobility of young people.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The present land is ancestral property; sacred places are linked to it, such as the watering place where game was hunted.
Having come from Sudan, the Moundang stayed at Léré (Chad), with which they share the harvest festival, initiation and kingship.
Relations with neighbours remain marked by the conflicts of history and by disputes between farmers and herders or over land.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The gon (king) governs with 11 notables (kaigama, alkali, kola…) and a clergy; castes are distinguished (hunters, seers, diviners, blacksmiths), as well as gender, kinship and land ownership.
In politics, the gon decides after consultation; in the family, the head of the family decides; at clan level, consensus is sought.
The Banjéré society leads the initiation (kane) to the yang, the guinarou initiation, choosing from among the bravest.

Deference: the woman bows to hand an object to a man and does not stare at her husband; children greet their elders, who serve themselves first; sons-in-law and daughters-in-law do not joke with their in-laws.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the young woman joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man at around 18 (deep voice, build); the girl becomes a woman at around 17, with puberty.
Formerly, a hoe or a bundle of firewood for the wife's first cooking was enough; today, one “knocks at the door” with a sum of money. The parents' choice has given way to free choice.
Steps: choice, inquiry by the families, negotiation, “knocking at the door”, purchase of plates, then bride price (often long to pay off).
The wrapper offered to the mother-in-law thanks her for having carried her daughter; the goat is intended for the maternal uncles; the plates entrust the household to the young wife.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Ancestor cult near the granaries; twin cult (millet stalk, water calabash, three dance turns around it); food offerings to the dead in the bush, by the guinarou.
Harvest festival (nezabère) in October–November and sesame cult to celebrate abundance.
Sacred places: the yang forest, in Kaélé, for the guinarou; the dadde, a heap of large stones near Diboma, a place of divine justice where one clears oneself of blame.
The heir is eagerly awaited, a gift from God; a boy of about ten years should no longer stay with his mother.
Death takes one back to the ancestors, but the spirits remain among the living (dreams, incantations).
Taboos: the secrets of the guinarou, incest (curse lifted by the calabash rite, zaiyé), the clan of the returning dead (ban mujere). Striking one's parents, adultery and murder are serious offences.
Divination by diviners (pakendang).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, hunting, crafts. Women: trade, farming, crafts.
The land belongs to the head of the family; it is inherited from the ancestors or cleared in order to own it.
Ancestral crafts of weavers and blacksmiths: bamteri cloth, mbolori hat against the sun, kapáá hoe, arrows.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly, a bamboo loincloth (tijeli) and bamteri breeches; today, jackets and boubous for men, wrappers for women.
Strong trust in traditional medicine, which is inexpensive and rooted in belief.
Beauty: strength, speed, agility, height and courage for men; medium height and build for women.
Courtship: dance, glances, smiles, song; it is the woman who offers gifts to the man.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances and rhythms: nade, bloum, dalanga, wigou, mawouli, daderkoum.
Instruments: tam-tam, flute, calabash, millet-stalk sticks.
Festival: Gbeza, every two years in June.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The first chief of Kaélé was Gongouré.
The Moundang show similarities with the Toupouri, the Gbaya and the Mboum.

sections.title: The names
items: Men's first names often begin with P-, W- or D- (Wassoue, Datoukouri, Wakile, Patouki, Padeu), women's with M- (Massoue, Matoukouri, Mahile, Matouri, Madou); twins: Seini (boy), Massing (girl).
The name tells the circumstances: born in the bush, Patouki or Matouri; born on the road, Wahile or Mahile.
People call each other by their own name, which does not change.
The founding ancestor is Gongoore, chief of Goore.

lessons.title: Who are the Moundang (Kaélé)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Moundang (Kaélé) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: << where the monitor lizard lives, the monitor lizard's bush >>

lessons.competence: Introduce the Moundang (Kaélé) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Moundang (Kaélé) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Moundang (Kaélé) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Moundang (Kaélé) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Moundang (Kaélé) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group, neighbour of the Guiziga, the Fulani and the Toupouri, many of whom also speak Toupouri, fulfulde and Guiziga. • Moundang is also spoken in Chad. • Long endogamous (exogamy was refused until around 1950), the group opened up after independence with the mobility of young people. • The present land is ancestral property; sacred places are linked to it, such as the water point where game was hunted. • Having come from Sudan, the Moundang stayed at Léré (Chad), with which they share the harvest festival, initiation and kingship.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority around Kaélé (“near the water”), the Moundang live alongside the Guiziga, Fulani and Toupouri. Coming from Sudan via Léré, in Chad, with which they share festivals, initiation and kingship, they obey a sovereign, the gon, surrounded by eleven notables. The guinarou, a great male initiation, and the biennial Gbeza festival punctuate their lives.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Moundang (Kaélé) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Moundang (Kaélé)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Moundang (Kaélé), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Moundang (Kaélé).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Moundang (Kaélé), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Moundang (Kaélé).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: white beans (lye), sesame (same), red millet (so'ozinuri), dried okra (lihiake), melon leaves (gokouare). • Drinks: bil-bil (himsore), millet beer. • Men: farming, hunting, crafts. Women: trade, farming, crafts. • The land belongs to the father of the family; it is inherited from the ancestors or cleared in order to own it.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Moundang (Kaélé) eat mainly white beans, sesame, red millet, dried okra. Traditional drinks: bil-bil (himsore), millet beer. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Moundang (Kaélé): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Marriage and bride price among the Moundang (Kaélé)
objectives: Putting the stages of marriage in order
Explain the symbolism of the bride price
lessons.competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Moundang (Kaélé) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.
lessons.situation: Your elder brother wants to marry a young Moundang (Kaélé) woman. What steps will he have to follow?
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, props for the staging.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the stages of the traditional Moundang (Kaélé) marriage, the elements of the bride price and their symbolism.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your older brother wants to marry a young Moundang (Kaélé) woman. Which steps will he have to follow?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who chooses the spouse? Do people marry within the group or outside it? — What are the stages of marriage? — What does the bride price include, and what does each item symbolise? — Where does the couple live after the marriage?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

activities.instruction: In groups, act out the marriage proposal.

activities.title: I reflect
activities.instruction: What has changed in marriage today?

student.memo: Steps: choice, inquiry by the families, negotiation, “knocking at the door”, purchase of plates, then bride price (often long to pay off).

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Moundang (Kaélé)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Moundang (Kaélé), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Moundang (Kaélé) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Moundang (Kaélé), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Moundang (Kaélé) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Dances and rhythms: nade, bloum, dalanga, wigou, mawouli, daderkoum. • Instruments: tam-tam, flute, calabash, millet-stalk sticks. • Festival: Gbeza, every two years in June.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Moundang (Kaélé), traditional dances (nade, bloum, dalanga) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, flute, calabash, millet stalks. Festival(s): Gbeza, nezabère.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Moundang (Kaélé) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover the music and dances of the Moundang (Kaélé), then learn to perform one.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Moundang (Kaélé), traditional dances (nade, bloum, dalanga) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, flute, calabash, millet stalks. Festival(s): Gbeza, nezabère.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Moundang (Kaélé)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Moundang (Kaélé), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Moundang (Kaélé). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Moundang (Kaélé), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Moundang (Kaélé). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, hunting, crafts. Women: trade, farming, crafts. • Land belongs to the head of the family; it is inherited from the ancestors or cleared in order to own it. • Ancestral crafts of weavers and blacksmiths: bamteri cloth, mbolori hat against the sun, kapáá hoe, arrows.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, hunting, crafts. Women: trade, farming, crafts. Land belongs to the father of the family; it is inherited from the ancestors or cleared in order to own it.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Moundang (Kaélé)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover how the Moundang (Kaélé) make a living from their work.

activities.title: I classify

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain how one obtains land to cultivate.

activities.title: I calculate
activities.instruction: Imagine the calendar of a working year (seasons, harvests, festivals).

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, hunting, crafts. Women: trade, farming, crafts. Land belongs to the father of the family; it is inherited from the ancestors or cleared in order to own it.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Moundang (Kaélé)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Moundang (Kaélé), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Moundang (Kaélé). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Moundang (Kaélé), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Moundang (Kaélé). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Ancestor worship near the granaries; twin worship (millet stalk, calabash of water, three dance circuits around it); food offerings to the dead in the bush, through the guinarou. • Harvest festival (nezabère) in October-November and sesame worship to celebrate abundance. • Sacred places: the yang forest, at Kaélé, for the guinarou; the dadde, a heap of large stones near Diboma, a place of divine justice where one clears oneself of blame. • The heir is eagerly awaited, a gift from God; a boy of about ten should no longer stay with his mother. • Death leads back to the ancestors, but spirits remain among the living (dreams, incantations).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestor cult near the granaries; twin cult (millet stalk, water calabash, three dance turns around it); food offerings to the dead in the bush, by the guinarou. Harvest festival (nezabère) in October-November and sesame cult to celebrate abundance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Moundang (Kaélé) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Moundang (Kaélé) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: Ancestor cult near the granaries; twin cult (millet stalk, water calabash, three dance turns around it); food offerings to the dead in the bush, by the guinarou. Harvest festival (nezabère) in October-November and sesame cult to celebrate abundance.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Moundang
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.langText: Wi or enè / we tchibe ne djambè ne doŋdjam Bene
vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Moundang (Kaélé) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Moundang (Kaélé) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Moundang (Kaélé) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Moundang (Kaélé) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Moundang. • Greetings: Soko = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mo or bene = morning greeting (one person); Wi or bene = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bueno, Gwè, Sey, Nay, Dappe. • The founding ancestor is Gongoore, chief of Goore. • The first chief of Kaélé was Gongouré.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Moundang are the first steps towards communicating with the Moundang (Kaélé). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Moundang.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Moundang are the first steps towards communicating with the Moundang (Kaélé). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
